summary:
This A/B evaluation covers five chat-task evals (3 iterations each) testing EKS overlay behaviors: delta classification, identity mismatch handling, vulnerability/CVE reporting, fleet drift, and overlay-not-requested handling.

Overall pattern: across four of the five evals (delta-classification, vuln-no-invented-cve, fleet-drift, overlay-not-requested), with_skill met the expected output notably more often than without_skill — in several cases without_skill scored 0/3 on expected output and 0/9 or near-zero on assertions, while with_skill passed roughly half to most of its assertions. In the fifth eval (identity-mismatch), both variants met the expected output 3/3, with with_skill passing all 9 assertions and without_skill 8/9 — a case where the two were close, with with_skill slightly ahead.

Looking within the assertions, many are flagged "flaky" rather than consistently passing or failing for either variant, meaning results varied across the 3 repeated runs for one or both variants — this tempers confidence in the magnitude of the gaps. A few assertions were "always_passes" for both variants (e.g., not computing New/Resolved/Regressed classes, and not silently skipping the delta overlay), meaning they don't differentiate the variants. Confidence levels backing these per-assertion and expected-output judgments were mostly "high," with a couple of "medium" cases (notably identity-mismatch and vuln-no-invented-cve expected-output judgments), so the measurements themselves are reasonably but not uniformly solid.

Trigger-fired rates (measured once, not per-variant) were low for identity-mismatch (1/3) and vuln-no-invented-cve (1/3), and moderate for fleet-drift and overlay-not-requested (2/3 each), only reaching 100% for delta-classification. Since trigger_fired applies before either variant's output is judged, these low rates mean fewer underlying runs actually exercised the behavior under test in several evals, which limits how much weight the expected-output and assertion results in those evals can bear.

On cost and runtime, with_skill consistently ran longer and cost more than without_skill across all five evals (e.g., 11s/$0.10 vs 7s/$0.06 on delta-classification; 16s/$0.14 vs 8s/$0.07 on fleet-drift; and cases where without_skill logged 0s/$0.00, suggesting it may have taken a shortcut or non-executing path on some runs). Context window utilization was similar and low for both (roughly 4-5%) with no compaction events.

Quality-comparison pairs (direct side-by-side quality judgments) were mostly skipped due to lack of comparable pairs — only one pair was evaluated, in the identity-mismatch eval, where that single comparison favored with_skill on accuracy and actionability, with completeness rated comparable; confidence on this was medium and based on just one pair, so it carries limited weight.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was measured only where data was available for one variant per eval: without_skill showed "mostly_consistent" results in four evals (identity-mismatch, vuln-no-invented-cve, fleet-drift, overlay-not-requested), while with_skill's consistency was only measured in delta-classification, where it came out "inconsistent" (score 1.33/above threshold, with 2 of 3 dimensions inconsistent). Because consistency data is largely non-overlapping between variants (missing for with_skill in four evals and for without_skill in one), a direct consistency comparison across the full set isn't possible from this data.

In sum: with_skill met expected outputs and passed assertions more often in four of five evals, often by a wide margin, while being slower and more costly to run in every eval; the fifth eval showed both variants performing well and closely matched. Many assertions showed flaky (run-to-run varying) pass patterns for one or both variants, and trigger-fire rates were low in several evals, which limits confidence in how representative these results are. Direct quality comparisons and consistency comparisons each had very limited overlapping data, so those dimensions provide only a partial, lower-confidence picture rather than a decisive signal.

eks-overlay-delta-classification.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat-task eval with 3 runs per variant, testing whether the agent correctly classifies finding statuses (Resolved/Persisting/Regressed/New/Unverified) and correctly describes matching methodology and report structure in a security-review delta scenario.

Trigger behavior: the behavior under test fired in all runs for both variants (3/3), so the eval condition itself is not in question.

Expected output (overall task success): with_skill met the expected output in 2/3 runs (67%), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%). Both measurements are backed by high-confidence judgments, so this is a clear, well-supported gap favoring with_skill at the whole-task level, though note it's based on only 3 runs each.

Per-assertion results (12 assertion-instances each, 4 distinct assertions x 3 runs):
- Overall pass rates: with_skill 9/12 (75%) vs without_skill 3/12 (25%).
- On every one of the 4 distinct assertions, with_skill's pass rate was equal to or higher than without_skill's — there is no assertion where without_skill outperformed with_skill, and no assertion passed by neither (so each assertion is discriminating and worth keeping).
- Two assertions (status classification, and Unverified-vs-Resolved distinction) show a smaller gap, with with_skill at 100%/67% vs without_skill at 67%/33%.
- Two assertions (fingerprint-based matching methodology, and placement of the delta in a 'Change since previous review' subsection) show a larger gap, with with_skill at 67% each and without_skill at 0% — without_skill never satisfied these in any of its 3 runs.
- All four assertions are flagged as "flaky" patterns, meaning results varied across runs for at least one variant rather than being fully consistent — so even with_skill's passes were not uniform run-to-run.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was faster (7s avg vs 11s avg) and cheaper ($0.06 vs $0.10 avg) than with_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.0% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either. So without_skill's lower cost/latency comes alongside substantially weaker correctness and completeness on this task.

Quality comparison: no side-by-side quality pairs were actually evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality-preference signal to weigh here — this dimension is absent data, not a tie or a loss for either variant.

Output consistency: with_skill was rated "inconsistent" overall (score 1.33, with 2 of 3 consistency dimensions rated inconsistent and 1 mostly consistent), based on high-confidence judgments — meaning with_skill's own outputs varied noticeably across repeated runs despite its higher pass rates. Variant_a has no consistency rating recorded (null), so no comparison is possible on this dimension for without_skill; this is missing data rather than a sign of good or bad consistency.

Overall picture: with_skill met the expected output and individual assertions more often, with no assertion where without_skill did better, but this comes at a higher runtime/cost and with_skill's own outputs were flagged as inconsistent across runs. Variant_a was faster and cheaper but failed the overall expected output in all 3 runs and scored much lower on assertions, including two assertions it never passed. No quality-preference data exists to further weigh the tradeoff, and sample size (3 runs) is small, so these findings, while directionally clear on correctness, should be read with that limited sample size in mind.

eks-overlay-delta-identity-mismatch.summary:
This eval looked at a single chat scenario run 3 times for each variant, focused on how the agent handles a delta/diff report between two environments (prod-a vs prod-b) when identity (account/region/cluster) doesn't match.

Trigger and expected output: The underlying trigger condition only fired in 1 of 3 runs overall (33%), which limits how much weight can be placed on findings here — most of the comparison rests on a small, partially-triggered sample. Both with_skill and without_skill fully met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%), with medium confidence in that judgment (not low, but not high either) and no low-confidence instances flagged.

Assertions: Most assertions behaved the same for both variants. Two of the three assertions always passed for both with_skill and without_skill (the response correctly avoids computing New/Resolved/Regressed classes, and it correctly surfaces a "not available / identity mismatch" message rather than silently skipping the section) — these are consistent behaviors that don't differentiate the variants. The third assertion, that the response states the delta requires a prior report for the same account/region/cluster, passed 3/3 for with_skill but only 2/3 (67%) for without_skill, flagged as "flaky" — this is the one point of divergence, with without_skill occasionally omitting or not clearly stating that requirement. Aggregate assertion pass rate was 9/9 (100%) for with_skill vs 8/9 (89%) for without_skill, driven entirely by that one flaky assertion.

Metrics: with_skill took about 3 seconds and cost about $0.03 per run on average; without_skill was reported at 0s runtime and $0.00 cost, with similar (slightly lower) context window utilization. The 0s/$0 figures for without_skill are unusual and may reflect a measurement artifact (e.g., a cached or skipped execution) rather than true zero-cost processing; this should be read cautiously rather than as a confirmed cost/speed advantage.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 3 pairs could be directly compared for quality (2 were skipped, likely due to the trigger not firing). In that single comparable pair, with_skill was favored on accuracy and actionability, while completeness was rated comparable between the two. Given only one pair was evaluated, this is a weak signal rather than a robust quality difference, and confidence was medium.

Output consistency: Consistency data exists only for without_skill, which was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33, medium confidence) across repeated runs. No consistency data is available for with_skill, so no comparison can be made on this dimension.

Overall state: The two variants are largely similar — they agree on 2 of 3 assertions and on meeting the expected output in all observed runs. The main observed difference is one flaky assertion (prior-report requirement) where without_skill underperformed with_skill in 1 of 3 runs, and a single-pair quality comparison favoring with_skill on accuracy/actionability. However, these findings are based on very limited data: only 1 of 3 trigger events fired, only 1 quality pair was evaluable, and the runtime/cost figures for without_skill look atypical and may not be reliable. This should be treated as a tentative, low-sample comparison rather than a firm conclusion.

eks-overlay-vuln-no-invented-cve.summary:
This evaluation ran a single chat-task eval across 3 repeated runs per variant, examining whether a specific triggered behavior (a vulnerability-posture overlay in a cluster snapshot) fired and met expectations.

Trigger and expected output: The underlying behavior under test only fired in 1 of 3 runs overall (33%), meaning for most runs there was nothing to evaluate against the expected output — this limits how much weight the expected-output numbers can bear. When it did get evaluated, with_skill met the expected output in 1/3 runs (33%) and without_skill in 0/3 runs (0%). Confidence behind these judgments was medium for both, and not based on low-confidence ratings, but the small sample (3 runs, with the trigger only firing once) means this gap should be read as a limited-data signal rather than a strong, well-established difference.

Per-assertion detail: Across 12 assertion checks, with_skill passed 6/12 (50%) and without_skill passed 3/12 (25%). Looking at the individual assertions:
- One assertion ("labels the vpc-cni lag as a version gap, not a confirmed vulnerability") passed 3/3 for both variants — this check is not distinguishing between the two.
- Three other assertions (about covering AWS-hosted add-on images with bulletin references, placing the summary in a "Vulnerability posture" subsection, and stating the overlay adds no new reads) each passed only 1/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill, and are flagged as "flaky" patterns. These show a consistent direction favoring with_skill, but the absolute pass rates are low for both variants (mostly failing), suggesting the underlying behavior itself is inconsistently produced regardless of variant.

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs could be evaluated (0 of 3 pairs compared; all 3 skipped), so there is no quality-based signal to weigh here at all.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~5s and ~$0.05 per run, while without_skill averaged ~0s and ~$0.00, with similar (low) context window utilization for both (~4-4.5%) and no compaction events. This suggests without_skill may be taking a much lighter-weight or possibly short-circuited path, which — combined with its 0/3 expected-output pass rate — could indicate it's doing less work rather than being simply more efficient, though this is speculative given the limited data.

Output consistency: without_skill showed "mostly consistent" outputs across repeated runs (score 2.67/3, high confidence), with 2 of 3 dimensions fully consistent. with_skill has no consistency data reported (null), so no comparison is possible on this dimension.

Overall state: The data available is sparse — the trigger behavior fired in only 1 of 3 runs, no quality comparisons were possible, and consistency data exists for only one variant. Within that limited data, with_skill shows higher expected-output and assertion pass rates than without_skill, but at the cost of more runtime and spend; one assertion shows no difference at all, and several others, while directionally favoring with_skill, have low absolute pass rates for both variants, pointing to a possibly flaky or hard-to-trigger behavior rather than a clear-cut variant difference.

eks-overlay-fleet-drift.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task run 3 times per variant, with a mix of trigger, expected-output, assertion, cost/runtime, quality-comparison, and consistency measurements.

Trigger & expected output: The behavior-under-test fired in 2/3 runs overall. On the expected-output check, with_skill met expectations in 2/3 runs (67%) while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%). Both variants' expected-output judgments were made with high confidence, so this gap is measured with reasonably solid confidence, not a low-confidence artifact.

Assertions: Across 5 distinct assertions (15 total checks), with_skill passed 12/15 (80%) and without_skill passed 3/15 (20%). All five assertions are individually flagged as "flaky" (pass rate varies across the 3 repeated runs for at least one variant), meaning neither variant's behavior was fully deterministic on this task. Looking at individual assertions: with_skill passed one assertion (AX10 classification) consistently (3/3) and without_skill also did reasonably on that same assertion (2/3) — this is the one case where both variants performed closer together. On the other four assertions, with_skill passed more often (ranging 2/3 to 3/3) while without_skill passed rarely or never (0/3 to 1/3), indicating a consistent gap across most individual checks rather than just in the aggregate. No assertion passed for neither variant, but none passed perfectly for both either.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was faster (~8s vs ~16s) and cheaper (~$0.07 vs ~$0.14) than with_skill, roughly half in both dimensions. Context window utilization was low for both (4-5.5%) with no compaction events for either.

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs could be evaluated (0 of 3 pairs evaluated, all 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality-preference data to weigh here — this dimension is effectively absent rather than showing parity.

Consistency: Output consistency was only computed for without_skill, which scored "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33, with 1 run rated fully consistent and 2 rated mostly consistent, high confidence). No consistency data is available for with_skill, so no direct comparison can be made on this dimension.

Overall, the clearest signal in this run is that with_skill met the expected output and individual assertions substantially more often than without_skill, with high-confidence judgments, while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper to run. Quality-comparison data and with_skill consistency data are both missing, limiting how fully this result can be weighed, and the "flaky" labeling on all assertions indicates some run-to-run variability in both variants' behavior on this task.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 2/3 runs (67%), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%). Both measurements are backed by high-confidence judgments, so this gap is a reasonably solid finding rather than noise, though it's based on only 3 runs.

All three assertions are marked "flaky" in pattern, meaning results varied across runs rather than being stable one way or the other, and all judgments were high confidence. Notably, every assertion that passed did so only for with_skill, and none passed consistently (3/3) for either variant — so even with_skill's better showing is not fully reliable.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs were evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality between the variants for this task.
